rationale: The speaker was peaceable with people who hated peace and fought him without cause. Romans instructs its readers to live peaceably if possible and as far as it depends on them and to answer an enemy's need with good. The comparison joins peaceful conduct with continued hostility, preserving report and instruction as different forms.

relationship: The contrast with a sleeping deity
rationale: The psalm denies both slumber and sleep of Israel's guardian. Elijah's mockery suggests that Baal might be asleep. The particular contrast concerns a deity's sleeping, with Elijah's words retained as mockery rather than a factual account of Baal.

relationship: The Lord at the right hand
rationale: The Lord will guard the addressee and is shelter at the right hand. Psalm 15 places the Lord at the speaker's right hand so that he may not be shaken. The divine position and protective result correspond, without adding shelter wording to Psalm 15.

The speaker recounts rejoicing over those who said they would go to the Lord's house. Isaiah portrays many nations inviting one another to go up to the Lord's mountain and the house of Jacob's God. Both concern a journey to God's house, with the reported resolve and the invitation distinguished.

The psalm describes hostile people conditionally swallowing the speakers alive. Proverbs quotes a murderous invitation to swallow a righteous man alive like Hades. The unusual image of swallowing a living victim connects the texts; the target's singular victim and Hades comparison remain distinct.

The psalm blesses the Lord for not giving the speakers as prey to enemies' teeth. Job recounts crushing unjust people's molars and tearing plunder from between their teeth. The shared predatory-teeth image links the Lord's withholding of prey and Job's removal of plunder, with their objects kept distinct.

relationship: The city and freedom from shaking
rationale: Those trusting in the Lord are compared with Mount Zion, and the Jerusalem dweller will never be shaken. Psalm 45 describes God's city as unshaken because God is in her midst. Both connect the city with freedom from shaking, but the source speaks of its dweller and the target of the city itself; the source also compares trusting people with Mount Zion.

The Lord will not leave sinners' rod upon the righteous person's lot. Isaiah says God shattered the sinners' and rulers' yoke. Both depict God ending sinful domination represented by an instrument of oppression; rod and yoke remain different images.

The source ends its judgment concerning tangled ways with peace upon Israel. Galatians pronounces peace and mercy upon those who will keep in step with its rule and upon the Israel of God. The explicit peace blessing connects the passages without equating their preceding judgments or defining their groups beyond the wording.

The psalm reports a mouth filled with joy and a tongue with exultation. Bildad forecasts God filling the mouth of true people with laughter and their lips with thanksgiving. The common image of a filled mouth is compared without endorsing Bildad's explanation of Job's suffering.

The source says the Lord has done great things with the speakers and they became glad. Mary says the Mighty One has done great things for her. The declaration of great divine acts is shared, with the communal and individual recipients distinguished.

The source calls sons the Lord's inheritance and the reward of the fruit of the womb. Jacob identifies his children as those with whom God has shown mercy to His servant. Both associate children with divine benefit, while the source's inheritance and reward remain its own terms.

The source wishes for the Lord's blessing from Zion, while Psalm 133 declares that He will bless from Zion. Psalm 127 additionally wishes that the person see Jerusalem's good things through life; Psalm 133 additionally identifies the Lord as maker of heaven and earth. The shared blessing formula remains precise.

relationship: Rooftop grass as an image of weakness
rationale: The source wishes Zion's enemies to become rooftop grass that dried up before it was pulled out. The oracle concerning Sennacherib compares weakened city inhabitants with rooftop grass among other images. The unusual rooftop-grass comparison is shared, with different subjects and the psalm's drying clause preserved.

relationship: A contrasting blessing at the harvest
rationale: The source says passersby have not spoken the divine blessing, following the barren grass image. Ruth narrates Boaz greeting reapers with the Lord's presence and their reply asking the Lord to bless him. The harvest setting and divine blessing create a contrast between an absent greeting and an exchanged one.

The source says atonement is with the Lord. Psalm 64 says God will make atonement for the speakers' impieties after words of lawless deeds overpowered them. The shared atonement claim connects both passages' response to lawlessness.

relationship: David's dwelling and the ark's lodging
rationale: The source vows to withhold entry into David's own house and bed until a place is found for the Lord. The account in 2 Samuel contrasts David already dwelling in a cedar house with the ark remaining in a tent. Both juxtapose David's lodging and God's dwelling, with the differing circumstances preserved.

relationship: Bowing at the place of God's feet
rationale: The speakers say they will bow toward the place where God's feet stood. Psalm 98 commands bowing at His footstool. Both locate worship through the image of God's feet, with place and footstool distinguished.

The image names ointment upon Aaron's head, descending upon his beard and his garment's border. Leviticus narrates Moses pouring anointing oil on Aaron's head and consecrating him. Aaron, oil and the head identify the connection; the ointment's descent upon the beard and garment's border is a detail of the psalm.

relationship: Dew as an image of divine blessing
rationale: The source compares the blessing scene with Hermon's dew descending upon Zion's mountains, where the Lord commanded blessing and life. Hosea depicts the Lord as dew to Israel, followed by blossoming and rooting. Dew associated with life and blessing from God connects the images without equating their geography.

Both describe God bringing clouds from the earth's extremity and making lightning for rain. The source says He brings winds from His treasuries; Jeremiah says He brought light from His treasuries. The shared sequence is retained with the different final objects and verb forms.

The source summarizes the Lord's striking Egypt's firstborn from human to beast. Exodus narrates the midnight blow against firstborn, from Pharaoh's firstborn to the captive woman's, and includes the firstborn of livestock. The firstborn judgment and its human-and-animal scope are particular.

The psalm credits the Lord with striking nations and killing powerful kings. The account in Joshua introduces the kings whom Joshua and Israel killed and the land allotted to Israel. The conquest summary corresponds, preserving the psalm's divine attribution and the narrative's human agents.

relationship: Sihon and Og named among defeated kings
rationale: Both name Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan among conquered rulers. The account in Joshua specifies their territories, while the psalm also includes all Canaan's kingdoms. The two named kings and realms give a precise historical connection.

The source says the idols have no breath in their mouth. Jeremiah describes falsely cast objects with no spirit in them. Both portray manufactured idols as lacking animating capacity, with breath in the mouth and spirit in them retained as distinct expressions.

The source recalls the striking of Egypt with their firstborn. Exodus describes the Lord striking Egypt's firstborn at midnight, including human and animal groups. The firstborn blow is the concrete historical connection.

The source praises the striking of great kings. The account in Joshua introduces kings whom Joshua and Israel killed beyond the Jordan and lists the lands involved. The comparison concerns the defeat of kings, preserving the source's divine attribution and the narrative's named human agents.
